prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. My reasons are the same and I have tested them against the chair's questions. The entry answers a first-order question about who gains and loses from technological change and trade. It pairs a conceptual account of shifting labour demand (skill supply and demand, the race between education and technology, tasks) with simple, inspectable quasi-experimental designs on local labour markets. From a metascience standpoint, the maturity case is the point I weigh most. The designs are transparent enough that the field has re-examined them for a decade or more: alternative specifications, instrument-validity and inference critiques of shift-share designs, extensions to other countries and periods. As I understand it, those exercises have refined magnitudes and heterogeneity and have not overturned the qualitative findings. The robust findings are slow adjustment, geographic concentration of costs, and weak reallocation out of exposed places. The contested findings are the overall size, the long-run persistence, and external validity beyond the US episode. I would anchor the citation on the robust findings and on the direction of the effects, and I would avoid any claim about a specific effect size. On the chair's question about what Katz contributes that can be cited, my answer is the supply-and-demand framework for returns to skill and the long-run evidence on the education-technology race. That is the long-run empirical backbone for why labour demand shifts, and it does not depend on the task model's theoretical priority. This is also why I want the citation worded around findings on labour demand, wages and local labour markets and not around the task model, where Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane are not credited here. The 2021, 2023 and 2024 labour, education and technology prizes lower the marginal case somewhat. They addressed different questions: causal methods, women's labour-market outcomes, and institutions and prosperity. None of them rewarded the distributional effects of technology and trade on wages and local labour markets. I do not treat the large number of members who prefer B027 as evidence of merit. The case rests on the evidence record and on whether one coherent citation can be written, and I think it can.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main weakness, and my exchange with colleagues has not removed it. The three-name cap leaves out Dorn, a central co-author of the trade-shock papers, and choosing Katz over Dorn depends on whether the citation covers one achievement or two. If the committee sees two prize-sized strands joined by Autor, a joint citation is hard to defend. Several of us have separately said that the task-model theory and the Goldin-Katz lineage overlap with already-recognised work and with scholars outside the credited set. The persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects remain debated, and the trade-shock strand could be judged strong applied work and not a prize-level conceptual advance. B006 has a cleaner originator pair, and I do not think it can be dismissed on identification grounds alone. My preference for B027 rests partly on a judgement about how much weight tested empirical confirmation deserves relative to attribution clarity. Reasonable members can weigh those differently.

responses.point: Friberg now credits Autor, Hanson and Katz, having moved from Autor, Dorn and Hanson in his opening. He argues that a trade-shock-only trio would credit one half of the achievement and that the citation should be worded around findings on labour demand, wages and local labour markets, not around the task model.
responses.response: I agree with both parts. His wording point is the one I now consider necessary: naming the empirical findings avoids claiming theoretical priority for a task framework whose full lineage is not credited. On the chair's question about which version I would accept if the other is not adopted, I would back Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a narrowed citation, for example 'for showing how import competition reshapes local labour markets and employment'. I would then expect the committee to accept that it is a smaller achievement, and I would be less confident about the prize-level claim for a single empirical shock. A two-name Autor-Hanson award is my least preferred version, because it removes both the skill-demand anchor and Dorn.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) prefers B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He regards the collateral-amplification mechanism as foundational, cleanly attributed and nearly thirty years old. He argues that it is distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and crises, and that B027's task and trade strands may need separate citations.
responses.response: I accept that B006 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and is not contested on maturity. His distinction from the 2022 prize is workable: a dynamic mechanism running through asset prices and collateral values, not bank runs or intermediation. I do not think the thin direct identification disqualifies it. It lowers my ranking, because a mechanism whose quantitative importance is established indirectly has had less direct public testing than the labour-demand findings. I have therefore replaced B018 with B006 as an alternative. B018 has no agreed three-name solution, and B006 is the stronger fallback if the committee decides B027 cannot be given a coherent citation. His point on the two-prize risk is the one I take most seriously. I think a citation worded around labour demand answers it, but I cannot say it removes the risk.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file prefers B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He moved from B012 on attribution and maturity grounds. He still lists the missing Dorn, the overlap with the Acemoglu and Goldin work, and the contested China-shock magnitudes as costs, and he doubts that B012's credit is cleaner.
responses.response: My round-1 reply to him addressed his opening two-name proposal, which his current file no longer holds, and I should say so. We now agree on the configuration. I share his concern that B012's credit is crowded by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum and that it sits next to the 2008 prize, so I keep it as an alternative, not a preferred option. It stays above B006 in my ordering because Helpman and Melitz are a mature pair with extensive empirical testing. His point that the magnitude critiques refine rather than overturn the finding is consistent with how I read the replication record. I would still say explicitly in the citation process that the effect sizes are not what is being rewarded.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first with Autor, Katz and Hanson. He treats the discovery as the easiest to state in a single citation, but warns that the task and trade strands may be two prize-sized achievements joined by a common author. He would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee narrows the citation to trade exposure.
responses.response: I agree that the two-achievements objection is the main risk to B027, and I can only partly answer it. The shared object across the strands is the wage and employment response of skill groups and places to shifts in labour demand. That supports one citation if it is worded around that outcome. It would not hold if the citation named a mechanism for each strand. I also agree with his readiness to accept the trade-only trio and I would join him in that case. It is a different citation, and it would put more weight on the part of the evidence where magnitudes are most contested. I would also keep his point that Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu sit outside the credited names, as a reason to avoid theory claims in the wording.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the technology and trade strands as one achievement or two. This decides between Autor-Hanson-Katz with a broad citation and Autor-Dorn-Hanson with a trade-adjustment citation.

Which China-shock findings are robust enough to anchor the citation. I regard the direction, regional concentration and slow adjustment as robust, and the magnitude, long-run persistence and external validity as still contested. I have not independently verified this and rely on my own reading of the literature.
How much the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes, and the credit owed to Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane outside the credited names, reduce the marginal case for the task and skill-demand strand.
Whether the weaker direct identification of B006 should rank it below broad, tested empirical work or whether clean attribution should outweigh it. I am unsure and could be persuaded either way.
Whether my weight on replication and transparent identification disadvantages mainly theoretical candidates unfairly.
statement.conflict_note: No change. None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited names in B027 or for my alternatives B012 and B006. My listed co-authors and ties (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak, Ellingsen, Johannesson, Brodeur) are not credited names on any of these ballots. My metascience background shapes how much I weigh replication and transparent identification. That is a perspective and not a connection. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
